intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that multiple endocrine neoplasia type V (MEN5) is caused by heterozygous germline mutation in the MAX gene (154950) on chromosome 14q23.

checks.claim: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type V (MEN5) is caused by heterozygous germline mutation in the MAX gene.
checks.evidence_quote: multiple endocrine neoplasia type 5 (MEN5) caused by heterozygous inactivating germline MYC-associated factor X (MAX) mutations
checks.explanation: The abstract says MEN5 is caused by heterozygous germline MAX mutations.

checks.claim: The MAX gene is located on chromosome 14q23.
checks.evidence_quote: The only heterozygous variant identified was in MAX (NM_002382.5): c.145T>C, p.Ser49Pro.
checks.explanation: The paper names MAX but gives no chromosome location. 14q23 is the gene's standard location, so stating it only restates the gene the paper names.

paragraphs.text: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type V (MEN5) is an autosomal dominant tumor predisposition syndrome caused by germline mutation in the MAX gene. Pheochromocytoma, often bilateral and multiple, is the main tumor type, and paraganglioma also occurs. Some carriers also develop tumors in other endocrine tissues, mainly pituitary adenomas. The term MEN5 was proposed for this association by Seabrook et al. (2021).

checks.claim: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type V (MEN5) is an autosomal dominant tumor predisposition syndrome.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not state an inheritance pattern or call this autosomal dominant; it only reports familial occurrence.

checks.claim: MEN5 is caused by germline mutation in the MAX gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Germline MAX mutations are associated with PCs, ganglioneuromas, neuroblastomas, pituitary neuroendocrine tumors, and, possibly, parathyroid adenomas
checks.explanation: The abstract links germline MAX mutations to the multiple endocrine neoplasia phenotype.

checks.claim: Pheochromocytoma is the main tumor type in MEN5.
checks.evidence_quote: Family A has multiple individuals with PC (including bilateral and metastatic disease)
checks.explanation: Pheochromocytoma is prominent in both families, but the abstract does not explicitly call it the main tumor type.

checks.claim: Pheochromocytomas in MEN5 are often bilateral and multiple.
checks.evidence_quote: In Family B, the proband has bilateral and metastatic PC
checks.explanation: Bilateral PC is reported, but the abstract does not say the tumors are 'often' bilateral or multiple.

checks.claim: Paraganglioma also occurs in MEN5.
checks.evidence_quote: Pathogenic germline MAX variants are associated with pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL)
checks.explanation: The Context section states that MAX variants are associated with paraganglioma.

checks.claim: Some MAX mutation carriers develop tumors in other endocrine tissues, mainly pituitary adenomas.
checks.evidence_quote: Pathogenic germline MAX variants are associated with pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL), pituitary neuroendocrine tumors and, possibly, other endocrine and nonendocrine tumors.
checks.explanation: Pituitary tumors and other endocrine tumors are mentioned, but the abstract does not say pituitary adenomas are the main other endocrine tumor type.

checks.claim: Seabrook et al. (2021) proposed the term MEN5 for the association of germline MAX mutation with pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma and other endocrine tumors.
checks.evidence_quote: Multiple Endocrine Tumors Associated with Germline MAX Mutations: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 5?
checks.explanation: The paper raises MEN5 only as a question in its title and 'suggests' MAX is a new MEN gene; the draft presents this as a definite proposal.

paragraphs.text: Seabrook et al. (2021) reviewed patients with germline MAX variants who had pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma together with other endocrine tumors. They proposed that this association be called multiple endocrine neoplasia type 5 (MEN5).

checks.claim: Seabrook et al. (2021) reviewed patients with germline MAX variants who had pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma together with other endocrine tumors.
checks.evidence_quote: To report 2 families with germline MAX variants, pheochromocytomas (PCs) and multiple other tumors.
checks.explanation: The abstract reports 2 new families rather than a review of patients; any literature review is not described in the abstract.

checks.claim: Seabrook et al. (2021) proposed that the association of germline MAX variants with pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma and other endocrine tumors be called multiple endocrine neoplasia type 5 (MEN5).
checks.evidence_quote: Multiple Endocrine Tumors Associated with Germline MAX Mutations: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 5?
checks.explanation: The term is raised tentatively (with a question mark) rather than formally proposed.

paragraphs.text: Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) studied families with hereditary pheochromocytoma that had no mutation in the known susceptibility genes. In carriers of MAX mutations, pheochromocytomas were often bilateral, and some carriers had metastatic disease.

checks.claim: Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) studied families with hereditary pheochromocytoma that had no mutation in the known susceptibility genes.
checks.evidence_quote: there are familial cases without mutations in these known genes. We sequenced the exomes of three unrelated individuals with hereditary PCC (cases)
checks.explanation: The abstract implies the cases had no mutation in the known genes but does not say so directly. It describes them as unrelated individuals rather than as families.

checks.claim: In the MAX mutation carriers studied by Comino-Mendez et al. (2011), pheochromocytomas were often bilateral.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not mention bilateral tumours; this may be in the full text, but only the abstract was supplied.

checks.claim: Some MAX mutation carriers studied by Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) had metastatic disease.
checks.evidence_quote: suggested an association with malignant outcome
checks.explanation: The abstract only suggests an association with malignant outcome. It does not explicitly say that individual carriers had metastatic disease.

paragraphs.text: Burnichon et al. (2012) screened a large series of patients with pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma and found germline MAX mutations in a small proportion. The tumors were mainly pheochromocytomas and were often bilateral. Their catecholamine profile was noradrenergic or intermediate.

checks.claim: Burnichon et al. (2012) screened a large series of patients with pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma and found germline MAX mutations in a small proportion of them.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 12 cited papers. This is a 2008 paper by Schlisio et al. about KIF1Bbeta, not Burnichon et al. (2012). It does not report screening for MAX mutations.

checks.claim: In the MAX mutation carriers reported by Burnichon et al. (2012), the tumors were mainly pheochromocytomas.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 12 cited papers. The abstract does not mention MAX mutation carriers or their tumor types.

checks.claim: In the MAX mutation carriers reported by Burnichon et al. (2012), the pheochromocytomas were often bilateral.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 12 cited papers. The abstract does not mention bilateral pheochromocytomas or MAX carriers.

checks.claim: The MAX-related tumors reported by Burnichon et al. (2012) had a noradrenergic or intermediate catecholamine profile.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 12 cited papers. The abstract does not mention catecholamine profiles.

paragraphs.text: Seabrook et al. (2021) reviewed the reported carriers of germline MAX variants. Besides pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, some carriers had pituitary adenomas, and other endocrine tumors were reported in a smaller number.

checks.claim: Seabrook et al. (2021) reviewed the reported carriers of germline MAX variants.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes 2 new families and does not mention a review of previously reported carriers; such a review may be in the full text, which was not supplied.

checks.claim: In the review by Seabrook et al. (2021), some germline MAX variant carriers had pituitary adenomas in addition to pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma.
checks.evidence_quote: Pathogenic germline MAX variants are associated with pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL), pituitary neuroendocrine tumors
checks.explanation: The association with pituitary tumors is stated, but not as the result of a review of reported carriers.

checks.claim: In the review by Seabrook et al. (2021), other endocrine tumors were reported in a smaller number of germline MAX variant carriers.
checks.evidence_quote: pituitary neuroendocrine tumors and, possibly, other endocrine and nonendocrine tumors.
checks.explanation: Other endocrine tumors are mentioned as a possible association, but not as the result of a review and with no indication of how many carriers were affected.

paragraphs.text: MEN5 is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) found that in the families they studied, the disease was transmitted through the father, which suggested a parent-of-origin effect.

checks.claim: MEN5 is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not state the mode of inheritance.

checks.claim: Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) found that in the families with MAX mutations they studied, the disease was transmitted through the father.
checks.evidence_quote: suggested an association with malignant outcome and preferential paternal transmission of MAX mutations
checks.explanation: The abstract says paternal transmission was 'preferential' and only 'suggested'. The draft states more firmly that the disease was transmitted through the father.

checks.claim: Paternal transmission of MAX-related pheochromocytoma in the families studied by Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) suggested a parent-of-origin effect.
checks.evidence_quote: preferential paternal transmission of MAX mutations
checks.explanation: The abstract reports preferential paternal transmission but does not use the phrase 'parent-of-origin effect'.

paragraphs.text: Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) performed exome sequencing in unrelated patients with hereditary pheochromocytoma and identified germline mutations in the MAX gene. The tumors had lost the wildtype MAX allele, often through uniparental disomy of chromosome 14. MAX protein was absent from the tumors, which was consistent with MAX acting as a tumor suppressor. The tumors had a transcriptional profile that pointed to activation of MYC-related pathways.

checks.claim: Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) performed exome sequencing in unrelated patients with hereditary pheochromocytoma.
checks.evidence_quote: We sequenced the exomes of three unrelated individuals with hereditary PCC (cases)
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) identified germline mutations in the MAX gene in patients with hereditary pheochromocytoma.
checks.evidence_quote: We sequenced the exomes of three unrelated individuals with hereditary PCC (cases) and identified mutations in MAX, the MYC associated factor X gene.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly; because the cases are hereditary, the mutations are germline.

checks.claim: The MAX-mutant tumors studied by Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) had lost the wildtype MAX allele.
checks.evidence_quote: Absence of MAX protein in the tumors and loss of heterozygosity caused by uniparental disomy supported the involvement of MAX alterations in the disease.
checks.explanation: Loss of heterozygosity in the tumours means the wildtype allele was lost.

checks.claim: Loss of the wildtype MAX allele in the tumors studied by Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) often occurred through uniparental disomy of chromosome 14.
checks.evidence_quote: loss of heterozygosity caused by uniparental disomy
checks.explanation: The abstract mentions uniparental disomy but does not name chromosome 14 or say how often it occurred.

checks.claim: MAX protein was absent from the MAX-mutant tumors studied by Comino-Mendez et al. (2011).
checks.evidence_quote: Absence of MAX protein in the tumors
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Absence of MAX protein in MAX-mutant tumors was consistent with MAX acting as a tumor suppressor.
checks.evidence_quote: Absence of MAX protein in the tumors and loss of heterozygosity caused by uniparental disomy supported the involvement of MAX alterations in the disease.
checks.explanation: Absent protein plus loss of heterozygosity fits a tumour-suppressor role, but the abstract never uses the term 'tumor suppressor'.

checks.claim: The MAX-mutant tumors studied by Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) had a transcriptional profile pointing to activation of MYC-related pathways.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not describe a transcriptional profile of the tumours.

paragraphs.text: Burnichon et al. (2012) identified germline MAX mutations in patients with pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma from a large series. They confirmed that the tumors lacked MAX protein on immunohistochemistry.

checks.claim: Burnichon et al. (2012) identified germline MAX mutations in patients with pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma from a large series.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 12 cited papers. This paper reports KIF1Bbeta mutations, not germline MAX mutations, and it is not Burnichon et al. (2012).

checks.claim: Burnichon et al. (2012) confirmed by immunohistochemistry that the tumors of germline MAX mutation carriers lacked MAX protein.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 12 cited papers. The abstract does not mention MAX immunohistochemistry.

paragraphs.text: MAX is the obligate partner of MYC. Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) found that MAX-mutant tumors lost the wildtype allele, and proposed that losing MAX function deregulates the MYC-MAX-MXD1 network and drives tumor formation.

checks.claim: MAX is the obligate partner of MYC.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not describe MAX as the obligate partner of MYC; it only gives the gene's full name, 'MYC associated factor X'.

checks.claim: Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) found that MAX-mutant tumors lost the wildtype MAX allele.
checks.evidence_quote: loss of heterozygosity caused by uniparental disomy supported the involvement of MAX alterations in the disease
checks.explanation: Loss of heterozygosity means the tumours lost the wildtype allele.

checks.claim: Comino-Mendez et al. (2011) proposed that loss of MAX function deregulates the MYC-MAX-MXD1 network and drives tumor formation.
checks.evidence_quote: The involvement of the MYC-MAX-MXD1 network in the development and progression of neural crest cell tumors is further supported by the lack of functional MAX in rat PCC (PC12) cells and by the amplification of MYCN in neuroblastoma and suggests that loss of MAX function is correlated with metastatic potential.
checks.explanation: The abstract implicates the MYC-MAX-MXD1 network in tumour development and links loss of MAX function to metastatic potential. It does not say explicitly that loss of MAX deregulates the network to drive tumour formation.
